column1: What is the Singer-Nicholson model and what two key dynamic properties does it ascribe to membrane lipids?
column2: The fluid mosaic model (1972): membranes are two-dimensional fluids. Lipids undergo rapid lateral diffusion (~10⁻⁸ cm²/s) but slow, non-enzymatic transbilayer flip-flop (hours to days), maintaining leaflet asymmetry.

column1: Why is phosphatidylserine normally restricted to the inner leaflet, and what happens when it appears on the outer leaflet?
column2: ATP-dependent flippases maintain its inner-leaflet localization against flip-flop energetics; its appearance on the outer leaflet serves as a recognized apoptotic ('eat-me') signal.

column1: Using Born solvation theory, why is the lipid bilayer core nearly impermeable to ions?
column2: ΔG_partition = (q²/8πε₀r)(1/ε_membrane − 1/ε_water). Because ε_membrane (~2) is far lower than ε_water (~80), transferring a monovalent ion costs >50 kcal/mol, making spontaneous crossing negligible without transport proteins.

column1: Write the Nernst equation and state what it calculates.
column2: E_i = (RT/z_iF)ln([i]_out/[i]_in) ≈ (58 mV/z_i)log₁₀([i]_out/[i]_in). It gives the equilibrium membrane potential at which an ion's electrochemical potential is equalized across the membrane (net flux = 0).

column1: What is the electrochemical potential equation for an ion species, and what two driving forces does it combine?
column2: μ_i = μ_i⁰ + RT ln[i] + z_iFV_m. It combines the chemical potential (concentration gradient, RT ln[i]) with the electrical potential energy (z_iFV_m) to determine net transport directionality.

column1: What equation relates actual Gibbs free energy change to standard free energy change and reactant/product concentrations in a cell?
column2: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient. This lets cells drive reactions favorably by maintaining concentrations far from equilibrium, independent of ΔG° sign alone.

column1: Why does ATP hydrolysis release more free energy in vivo (~−50 kJ/mol) than under standard conditions (−30.5 kJ/mol)?
column2: Cells maintain high ATP/ADP ratios far from equilibrium; per ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, the low product-to-substrate ratio (Q << 1) makes the actual ΔG more negative than the standard value.

column1: What three factors make the ATP phosphoanhydride bond 'high energy'?
column2: (1) Electrostatic repulsion between adjacent negatively charged phosphate groups, (2) resonance stabilization of hydrolysis products (ADP + Pi), (3) favorable solvation entropy changes upon hydrolysis.

column1: Why is base-pairing thermodynamic stability (ΔΔG ≈ 2–5 kcal/mol) alone insufficient to explain DNA replication fidelity (~10⁻⁹–10⁻¹⁰ error rate)?
column2: Thermodynamic discrimination alone cannot achieve such low error rates; kinetic proofreading via exonucleolytic editing domains on DNA polymerases excises mismatched nucleotides, multiplying fidelity beyond simple base-pairing selectivity.

column1: What topological problem arises during DNA replication fork progression, and what invariant describes it?
column2: Unwinding generates positive supercoiling ahead of the fork and compensatory changes behind it, governed by the linking number invariant Lk = Tw + Wr (twist + writhe). Topoisomerases resolve this by transiently cutting and resealing DNA strands.

column1: Why does DNA replication require continuous leading-strand and discontinuous lagging-strand (Okazaki fragment) synthesis?
column2: DNA polymerase synthesizes only 5'→3', but the two template strands are antiparallel. One strand is copied continuously in the fork-opening direction (leading), while the other must be synthesized discontinuously in short fragments (lagging).

column1: What molecular 'clock' drives the cell cycle, and what are its two essential components?
column2: An oscillating biochemical clock built from cyclins (regulatory proteins with periodically rising/falling concentration) and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs, catalytic subunits active only when cyclin-bound), whose oscillating activity drives phase transitions and checkpoint control.
